title: Women in Buddhism
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk highlights the importance of women's participation and leadership in spiritual communities, drawing inspiration from the story of Maha Pajapati Gautami, a Buddhist woman who achieved enlightenment and played a significant role in establishing the order of nuns in early Buddhism. Her legacy serves as a powerful example of the value of women's contributions to spiritual growth and the transmission of the Buddha's teachings. This teaching emphasizes the need for humility, openness, and adaptability in approaching spiritual practice, recognizing that our understanding is always incomplete and subject to change.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
Many of us, this is the second talk of the evening.
A little earlier you did a lovely job introducing us to the Lotus Sutra, the vast cosmic vision of that style of Buddhist understanding.
Just reminding us that Buddhism is really a very, very wide tradition.
It's moved through many different cultures, many centuries, many countries, so it has many different expressions.

And to me, one of the great values of a wild, far-out expression like we'll learn about in the Lotus Sutra with Edie these next weeks is to soften up on whatever we think our view is and what the right way to look at it is, right?
Because how could there be a right way to look at it?
So tonight I'd like to share with you some stories about great Buddhist woman practitioners, two stories.
The first is a name that we chant in the morning service.
Prajapati or Prajapati or Maha Prajapati, Maha Prajapati.
Different languages, all these different layers.
Am I speaking loudly enough?
Is it okay?
Okay.
I'm mostly going to read a chunk of a chapter from Susan Murcott's wonderful book called First Buddhist Woman and just make a few comments.
And then I also have a story from Dogen about a Buddhist woman that he appreciated.
And I think I'm deliberately going to read slowly so you can just enjoy the sound of the words or your breath or the body and not worry about anything too much.

*Maha Prajapati Gautami, who was to become the founder of the first order of Buddhist nuns, was born in the Kaliya clan in the town of Devadaha in northeastern India near the foothills of the Himalayas.*
And she is going to have a big part of the story of the Buddha.
*At her birth, an astrologer foretold that she would be the leader of a large following.
And she was named Prajapati, meaning leader of a great assembly.
Maha is a prefix meaning great, which was used later with her name.
It was further prophesied of her, as it had been of her older sister Maya, that she would be the mother of a great secular or religious ruler.*
*Prajapati and her sister Maya grew up and were both married to a chief of the Sakya clan, Sudodhana.*
So the two sisters were married to the same man.
A little different social arrangements than in our society.
We usually marry two sisters.
We have a lot of stories about marrying the wrong sister, right?
In this society you could just marry them both.
*And they lived with their husband, Sudodhana, in the capital town of Kapilavastu.
According to Buddhist legend, Sudodhana was a great king, and his son, Siddhartha, was a prince and heir.
But in fact, the more historical fact is that in the Sakya clan, any male was eligible to be the chief, and it was a position elected by rotation.*
They were a little more democratic.
*The only true king, in our sense of the word, in the region was Pasanadi, the king of Kosala, who was the overlord of the states that included the Sakyan and Kolean clans.
Maya and Prajapati's marriage was into a clan very similar to their own.
Both clans were small and did not observe caste distinctions rigidly.
The clan members worked in agriculture, wielded arms when necessary, and traded in nearby provinces,* which is jobs that are separated in other contemporaneous Indian societies.
So as usual, when you learn more about something, it turns out to be more complicated.
There was a caste system in India, well established, even at this time.
It was about 500 or 600 BC.
Nobody knows exactly when.
But it wasn't implemented in the same way in different societies.
The society was relatively egalitarian.
*Maya was the first to become pregnant.
As was customary, Maya wanted to give birth in her family home.
So when her time was near, she undertook the journey to Devadaha, walking.
En route she stopped in the Lumbini garden to rest and admire the flowering trees.
There she raised her arm to pick a blossoming branch of an asoka tree, and she felt her initial labor pains and gave birth to a boy under the tree.*
And there's a footnote.
*Two centuries later, the Buddhist emperor, Asoka,*
same name as the tree,
*set up a pillar to mark that site, and that pillar survives to this day.*
So we know the exact location where this is supposed to have happened.
Maybe we'll all go there one day.
It would be great to go to India and go to the birthplace of the Buddha.
So this is the Buddha being born.

*When they heard the news back in Kapilavatthu, Suddhadana, and everyone else was overjoyed at the birth of a son, the chief immediately called a famous seer, Atisha, or Asita, who declared that if the child remained at home, he would become a secular ruler.
If he left home, he would become a great religious teacher of the Buddha.
The newborn was named Siddhartha, which means he who will accomplish his aim.
He who will accomplish his aim.
But seven days after her delivery, Maya died.
Neither history nor legend tells us why.
Pajapati took Siddhartha and raised him as her own first child, and later bore two more children, a daughter named Sundarinanda and a son named Nanda.*
The names are confusing.
The daughter is Sundarinanda, the son is.
*Years passed, and at the age of 29, Siddhartha left home and did not return during the six years of his religious quest.
His foster mother was now in her 50s or early 60s when Siddhartha finally came back to Kapilavatthu.
Upon his return, he was treated coolly.
His wife Yasodhara,*
whom Marty was sharing a piece about the other night, remember that, that was Yasodhara, so Pajapati's daughter-in-law,
*did not embrace him, but sent her son Rahula to meet him, their son, Rahula, to meet them.
The Sakyan clan was known for its pride in religious conservatism, so they were skeptical of the novel teachings of a once favorite son.
Pajapati no doubt would have been sensitive to all the varying reactions.
Her own response was to welcome him, and Sudhana did also.
And when the Buddha preached to them, both were moved by his teachings and became converts.*
She didn't talk about it much here, but there's also an early text about Yasodhara's reaction that wasn't so much referenced in the piece Marty read us.
Yasodhara was really pissed.
It was a long piece about how upset she was.
So these are parts of the Buddha story that are hard.
They're hard to understand.
They don't seem to quite fit our idea of what the Buddha would be or is or the teachings are.
And there's also a piece in the Pali Canon, actually it's in the Life of the Buddha book, where when Rahula goes up to welcome his father back, the Buddha ordains him on the spot, basically.
The way it's written, it seems a little manipulative.
It talks him into it.
You're a monk now.
So there's some difficult pieces in here, and it's going to get a little more difficult as Pajapati realizes that these teachings from Buddha mean a lot to her personally.
*By this time, Pajapati would not only have been eminent as the wife of the chieftain, but would also have been well respected for her age.
And after she became a lay convert to her son's new teachings, she may have been held in even greater esteem as a woman who had access to religious instruction and practice.
One by one or in groups, women started to seek out Pajapati's support, advice, and direction.
These women appealed to her not merely because of her high station.
She shared with them the particular anxiety of being a woman without any primary male relations.
Because,*
and this is interesting,
*following the Buddha's return to Kapilavatthu, Pajapati's son Nanda and her grand nephew Rahula, the son of Buddha, both became monks.
And not long after this, Suddhadana died.*
So the men in life are either dying or becoming monks, which removes them from the family and societal system.
Monks are outside society in this system.
*Though as seldom mentioned, Katama, besides leaving a wife and a child, also left a harem of women.*
And later in the book she talks more about the harem and what that means.
It's a little different from our movie ideas.
*The majority of the authors of the poems that she's going to talk about are women who were formerly of Siddhartha Katama's harem.
Women who lost their sense of identity and their position in society and ended up seeking out a spiritual life, setting out on a spiritual journey, but out of necessity.*
So in a way the Buddha was coming forward with these great teachings, and in a way he was really disrupting his society.
So we talk about disruption.
It's positive and negative both, right?
Cool technologies are supposed to be disruptive technologies.
Make us think in whole new ways and buy lots of stuff from Apple.
*Next a significant event occurred which brought even more women to Pajupati's door.
An angry dispute arose between the Sakhans and their neighbors, the Kalyans, over the right to draw water from the major river of the region.*
It's a resource issue.
*A battle ensued in which some men were killed and some women lost their husbands and came to Pajupati seeking support.
And other women went to the Buddha and urged him to try to settle the dispute.
The Buddha related not only to the Sakhans, but also through Maya and Pajupati was related to the Kalyans.*
So that's where they were from.
*And he delivered an inspiring sermon.
As a result of his dharma talk, many of the men renounced fighting altogether and became monks.*
So also, they may have all been killed.
They were now not husbands anymore, not fathers anymore.
They were monks.
*And this left yet another group of Sakhan and Kalyan women without husbands or other primary male relations.
Altogether, the number of women who came to Pajupati by this time totaled 500.*
500 is in quotes, and she explains,
*500 is a number frequently used to mean many.
No doubt, many came simply for comfort and support.*
And we know from the Lotus Sutra, 500 is not very many.
It could have been 100,000 or a million.
*500 women.
And many did come simply for comfort and support, but others came to resolve deep questions, deep questions about birth, suffering, and death.
And others sought a new family with women they trusted and with whom they shared common experience.
Belonging to these women, whatever form it took, became their spiritual aspiration.
All had personal stories, most of which are now lost to us, and all had their own experience of what the Buddha called the first noble truth.
This is what motivated them to join with Pajupati in a new and radical way that she was about to suggest.
Pajupati recognized that there was a powerful conjunction of events and people happening.
An old and influential woman without further worldly obligations, she was surrounded by displaced wives, widows, consorts, dancers, musicians.
Lacking other kin, these women were turning to her and to one another.
Having fully grasped the situation, Pajupati decided to take the following course, which is recounted in the Kula Vaga,*
which is part of the early writings about precepts, part of the precept writings.
*Now at one time, the Buddha was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan monastery.
Maha Pajupati Gatami went to him.
The place where the Buddha was, approached him and greeted him, and standing at a respectful distance, spoke to him.
It would be good, Lord, if women would be allowed to renounce their homes and enter into the homeless state under the Dharma and the discipline of the Tathagata.*
Meaning, it would be good if women could become nuns.
Can women become nuns?
*The Buddha said, enough Gatami.
Don't set your heart on a woman being allowed to do this.
A second and a third time, Pajupati made the same request in the same words and received the same reply,*
which is a big deal in this culture we learn from other Pali canon texts, that asking three times is a big deal.
You only would ask three times.
You really mean it.
It's different from us, right?
We would never even ask a second time.
Too embarrassing.
But here, it's understandable to ask one time.
They say, no, you ask again.
They'll say yes the third time.
But Buddha said no all three times, which is a big no, a really big no.
*And thinking that the Blessed One would not allow women to enter into homelessness, she bowed to him.
Keeping her right side towards him, she departed in tears.
Then the Blessed One set out for Vasali.*
And Pajupati, he moved on, left her behind.
*Pajupati cut off her hair, put on saffron-colored robes, and headed after him for Vasali with a number of Sakyan women.
She arrived at the Kuttigara hall in the great grove*
*with swollen feet, covered with dust.
Weeping, she stood there outside the hall.* This is source text.
It's a translation, of course, but this is what the text actually said.
She's crying.
*Seeing her standing there, the Venerable Ananda, as the Buddha's cousin and attendant, said, why are you crying?*

*Because Ananda, the Blessed One, does not permit women to renounce their homes and enter into the homeless state under the Dharma and discipline proclaimed by the Tathakata.* *Then the Venerable Ananda went to the Buddha, bowed before him and took his seat to one side.

He said, Pajupati is standing outside, under the entrance porch with swollen feet, covered with dust, and crying because you do not permit women to renounce their homes and enter into the homeless state.
It would be good, Lord, if women were to have permission to do this.* *Enough, Ananda.

Don't set your heart on women being allowed to do this.* *A second and a third time, Ananda made the same request in the same words and received the same reply.* Then Ananda thought, and this is like the great brainstorm in women's religious history.
*Then Ananda had a thought.
The Blessed One does not give his permission, so let me try asking on different grounds.
Are women able, Lord, when they have entered into homelessness to realize the fruits of stream entry, once returning, non-returning, and arhatship?* Those are the stages of practice.
So he's saying, are women, once they were to really enter into deep practice, are they able to be enlightened?
Can they do it?
Can they do the whole thing to the end?

*The Buddha said, yes, Ananda, they are able.* *Then, if women are able to realize perfection, and since Pajupati was of great service to you, she was your aunt, nurse, and foster mother, when your mother died, she even suckled you at her own breast.
It would be good if women could be allowed to enter into homelessness.*

*The Buddha said, if then Ananda Pajupati accepts the eight special rules, let that be reckoned as her ordination,* says the end of the quote from the Kula Vaga, and the eight rules are listed other places.
But essentially, I won't spend time on what all eight are, but essentially the eight rules give the nuns second class status in the assembly.
Like, fully ordained, but with various conditions that make them somewhat second class, but in the assembly nonetheless.
And this is back to Susan Murcott speaking.
*It must have been evident to the Buddha that Pajupati and the group of women with her had walked 150 miles barefoot.* So let's look to about, where would that be?
Olympia, I guess.
Maybe a little past Olympia.
So walked barefoot down I-5.
*Since they had done this, with their heads shaved, and the saffron colored robes of the already ordained, maybe he could just tell they weren't going to accept no for an answer.*
That's one possibility.
And this is something people have thought about for a long time.
He said no, he said yes with conditions, why?
Was the Buddha caught by the conditioning of his time?
There's some sexism baked in.
Was he just being skillful?
What was this?
It's an important question.
*Or the sight of these women and their unshakable sincerity must have made a vivid impression, not only on the sympathetic Ananda.
And their resolve was audacious in a culture where humility and obedience were the foremost traits in women.
Perhaps the eight special rules, the acceptance of which was a prerequisite to women's ordination, were a bulwark against any possible future boldness.* Maybe.

*Though the eight special rules clearly relegated women to a secondary status, Pajupati accepted them in order to achieve her primary goal of establishing an order of nuns.* *Later, in a story less frequently told,* and this is interesting, I didn't know this until recently, *Pajupati returned with a further request.
The implementation of this request would have annulled the first special rule, which required that the most senior nun bow down even to the most novice monk.*
And that's worth noting too that in this system you often were ordained very young, so like a 12-year-old boy.
So a senior, a seven-year, eight-year-old nun would be junior to a 12-year-old boy.
So in this section, Pajupati is talking to Ananda.
*I would ask one thing of the Blessed One, Ananda.

It would be good if the Blessed One would allow making salutations, standing up in the presence of others, paying reverence, and the proper performance of duties to take place equally between both monks and nuns, according to seniority.* *And the Venerable Ananda went to the Blessed One and repeated her words to him.
This is impossible, Ananda, and I cannot allow it.
Even those teachers of false dharma don't permit such conduct in relation to women.
How much less so can the Tathagata allow it?*
So Susan Murcott says, and this is a good point, *after being accepted as nuns, her attempt to change this first and most blatantly sexist rule.
In that action we can understand that she was not in sympathy with the discrimination that the rules reflected.
Her request also indicated a radical democratic orientation.
It comes in a time when even the most ancient Greeks who have been credited with founding democratic rule only allowed free, i.e. non-slave males, the privilege of citizenship.
Unfortunately, this is all we hear of the politics of the early order of nuns.*
*But we do know a little more about Pajapati.
Upon ordination, she received a subject of meditation, and through it was able to realize perfection.
She writes, I have reached the state where everything stops.* That is Neroda, the extinction of senses, feelings, and consciousness.
Just complete stability, letting everything drop.
*This achievement is synonymous with nirvana, the highest attainment.*
*And at a ripe old age of 120, Pajapati knew that her time of death was near.

And though it was against monastic regulations that a sick nun be visited by any monk,* one of the rules, *Pajapati requested that her foster son come to her, and by going, the Buddha in effect undermined his own rule.
When she died, miracles occurred, both then and at her cremation, miracles which later was said to have been equaled only by those that took place at the Buddha's own death.*
*Here the early sangha judged Pajapati as a very remarkable person.
When we consider Pajapati and her sister Maya, whom Pajapati mentions in the closing stanza of her poem,* so the poem's coming up, *we consider them as the great mothers of the Buddhist tradition.

For Maya, the mother of the Buddha, this is an obvious designation, but it's equally appropriate in describing Pajapati, who through countless lives had come to know all relations, mother, son, father, brother, grandmother.*
That's a reference to a poem coming up.
So the sense of many lives is interesting, and that's in the background of all of these teachings, Lotus Sutra teachings too.

And what's sort of freeing about that, whether or not you worry too much about the literal ideas about how could rebirth really be and stuff like that, but a sense of, we're not just in relationship with the rest of the world through the ages of our own current sort of limited understanding, we have the sense that we've been many different people in many different stations and relationships, and genders too, and genders too.
So it kind of frees us up.

So here's the poem, and so the basis of this wonderful book by Susan Murcott is to try to put together everything she could about the woman whose poems are collected in a section of the Pali Canon called the Terigata, and their enlightenment poems, awakening poems, and many of them are formulaic and kind of wonky to our ears, but they have names, they're titled, they have authorship.

So Susan Murcott in some of this I'm sure is somewhat speculative in her part, but she went to as many different sources as she could to try to find out what's the story with these women whose poems are listed with names, whether they wrote them or not, who knows.
So I'll close this part with Mahapajapati's poem.
*Amasya, you Buddha, best of all creatures, who set me and many others, who set me and many others free from pain.
All pain is understood.
The cause, craving, is dried up.
The noble eightfold path, way, unfolds.
I have reached the state where everything stops.
I've been mother, son, father, brother, grandmother, knowing nothing of the truth I journeyed on.
But I have seen the Blessed One.
This is my last body.
I will not go from birth to birth again.
Look at the disciples altogether, their energy, their sincere effort.
This is homage to the Buddhas.
Maya gave birth to Gautama for the sake of us all.
She has driven back the pain of the sick and the dying.*
*Amasya, you Buddha, best of all creatures, who set me and many others free from pain.
All pain is understood.
The cause, the craving, is dried up.
The noble eightfold way, unfolds.
I have reached the state where everything stops.
I have been mother, son, father, brother, grandmother, knowing nothing of the truth I journeyed on.
But I have seen the Blessed One.
This is my last body.
I will not go from birth to birth again.
Look at the disciples altogether, their energy, their sincere effort.
This is homage to the Buddhas.
Maya gave birth to Gautama for the sake of us all.
She has driven back the pain of the sick and the dying.*
It sounds beautiful in the ending with, did this great thing.

And the other thing to note about that story is one of the things that a few of us have gotten to speak with and meet the American Buddhist scholar, Paula Arai, who studies Japanese women, Japanese Buddhist women.
And she documented a very elaborate and wonderful ceremony that they do, the Buddhist women do in Japan, to thank Ananda for intervening in that story.
And they do it every year, and it's a big, important ceremony.
Isn't that amazing?
Yeah.
And that's one of the things you have to love about tradition.
I mean, sure, tradition bugs us a little bit as postmodern Americans, but there's something about keeping alive the gratitude about a story that's nearly 3,000 years old.
And here's a little bit from Dogen.
Dogen also was a great believer in women practitioners.
We don't really know, we know of one nun who studied with him and several lay women, and for sure, the monasteries he established were exclusively or mostly men.
So maybe that was just a function of what he could do in that cultural time and place, or who knows.
But he has one fascicle in Shobu Genzo that people usually quote where he talks directly about women practitioners.
It's called Raihai Tokusui.
Translation here of the title is receiving the marrow by bowing.
So receiving the marrow by bowing.
And it's like prostrations.
Raihai is prostrations.
Marrow, like the marrow.
It's an awkward translation.
I think there's no good way to translate it.
Receiving the essence.
Receiving the essence by bowing.
Yeah, thanks for asking.
Yeah, the mirror.
And it's typical of Dogen.
He doesn't really generalize about anything sort of discursive.
Like we would write a little essay and say, I believe women are fully worthy.
He doesn't really say that.
When Dogen generalizes, it's only about non-discursive things.
So it's really hard to understand.
He'll generalize about mountains walking, about all kinds of weird stuff.
But the way he makes points is by telling stories.
So our tradition is very much bound up in stories, the story we just heard.
And he tells several stories about enlightened women in this fascicle.
So that's how he's making this point.
So here's one of the stories.
*The nun Miao Xin, the Chinese nun, was a student of Yangshan.

When Yangshan was looking for someone to fill the position of the director of the guest house at the foot of Mount Yangshan, he asked his senior students, who had served as officers, to make a recommendation.
After some discussion, Yangshan said, although Miao Xin is a woman, she has heroic aspiration.
She should be suited to serve as the director of the guest house.
Everyone agreed, and Miao Xin was appointed to the position.
None of Yangshan's other students resented the decision, as it was not a minor position.*
So it's an important position.
And now in this system, in China, positions, like we're doing here, positions and jobs are very important, and that's how you practice.
Not so much about sitting under trees and attaining stream entry in Ramana and all this.
It's about doing the practice of running the monastery, doing the positions as practice.
And that's what Dogen really carried forward with his elaborate and lengthy instructions that he wrote down and gave orally.
So this is a certain vision of practice, a little different from Mahapajapati, a sort of communal practice.
So very similar to what we're doing.
So it's a big deal who we appoint to a position, right?
It matters.
It may seem completely haphazard here, but actually, carefully constructed.
Very carefully done.
So this woman was appointed to this position as the head of the guest house, which is kind of the public face of the monastery.
So it makes sense.
It would be a big deal.
*While Miao Shan filled this position, when she was in this position, there came a group of 17 monks from Shu in the west who were on the road in search of a master.
On their way to climb up Yang Shan's monastery, they stopped and stayed at the guest house.* So it's like through a gate house down below.
*Interested in the evening, they discussed the story about the wind and the banner of Huineng, high ancestor of Caoxi.
The 17 monks' interpretations were all wrong.* So they're talking about a Zen story.
*Miao Shan, who overheard the discussion from outside the room, said, how wasteful.
How many pairs of straw sandals have these 17 blind donkeys worn out?
They have never even dreamed of Buddha dharma.
Her assistant worker told them that Miao Shan had not approved their understanding.*
So it's not clear whether her assistant was supposed to tell them that.
Maybe, probably: "Go tell them."
*Instead of being upset with their disapproval, the monks were ashamed of their lack of understanding.
So they got formally dressed, offered incense, bowed and asked her to teach them.*
So that's surprising, huh?
*Miao Shan said, come closer.
When the 17 monks were still getting closer, Miao Shan said, it is not the wind that flaps.
It is not that the banner flaps.
It is not that your mind flaps.*
So the story in brief is, you see a flag waving.
This is a famous Zen story.
And the question is, is the flag moving or is the wind moving or is your mind moving?
We externalize and create reality in our culture because definitely it's the flag moving, right?
Another view is it's the mind moving.
And she's saying, well, neither, maybe.
*Hearing her words, all 17 monks had realization.
They thanked her and formally became her students.
Soon after, they went back to Shu without climbing up Miao Shan's monastery.*
So that's a big deal.
They didn't go and see the master.
They didn't go and see.
They were impressed by the teacher in the guest house, the woman teacher in the guest house.
*Indeed, this is nothing the Bodhisattvas of the three classes or ten stages can come up with.
It is work transmitted by Buddha ancestors from era to era.
Thus, even nowadays, when the position of abbot or head monk is not filled, you should request a nun who has attained Dharma to assume the position.
However aged or senior a monk may be, what's the use of someone who has not attained the way?
The master of an assembly should be a person of clear eye.
Those who are drowned in the body and mind of villagers are often so stubborn that even lay people may ridicule them.
It is not worth mentioning in Buddha Dharma.
Some refuse to bow to female teachers who have received Dharma transmission.
Because these people lack knowledge and study, they are close to animals and far from Buddha ancestors.
If such people are deeply determined to throw their body and mind wholeheartedly into Buddha Dharma, Buddha Dharma takes pity on them without fail.
Foolish humans and devas still have the capacity to feel the truth.
How should the authentic Dharma of all Buddhas not have compassion to respond to sincere hearts?
Even mud, rocks, sand and pebbles have hearts to be infected by sincerity.
Today nuns stay in monasteries of the Great Song of China.

When the attainment of Dharma by one of them is acknowledged and she is appointed abbess of a nunnery by the government, she ascends the teaching seat in the monastery where she is staying, all monks including the abbot assemble, stand and listen to her Dharma discourse.
Some monks ask questions.
This has been the custom since ancient times.*
This is historically revisionist somewhat on Dogen's part.
He's denying the eight special rules that we heard about in the first chapter.
He's saying no.
So his way of saying you should stop that bad behavior and listen to women teachers, his way of saying that is by saying monks have always listened to women teachers, whether they had or not.
*One who has attained Dharma is a true, authentic Buddha and should not be regarded as the same as before.
When we see the person, someone who is new and extraordinary sees us.
When we see the person today, sees today.*
That's interesting.
Let me read that again.
Dogen talked often about mutual recognition of Buddha Dharma.
*When we see the person, someone who is new and extraordinary sees us.
When we see the person today, sees today.

When arhats, pratyeka Buddhas or bodhisattvas of the three stages in ten classes come to a nun who maintains the treasury of the true Dharma, they should bow and ask about Dharma and she should receive their bow.
Why are men special?
Emptiness is emptiness.
Four great elements are four great elements.
Five skandhas are five skandhas.
Women are just like that.
Both men and women attain the way.
You should honor attainment of the way.
Do not discriminate between men and women.
This is the wondrous principle of the Buddha way.*
Yeah, and this is, so this is 12th century, right?
And I don't know for sure, I'm not aware that there are any extant writings from other Buddhist teachers of this period that go that far.
He only goes that far in one fascicle out of thousands of chapters of writing probably, but there it is.
And interestingly, he didn't, as far as we know, transmit the Dharma to any woman.
Six or seven, what time is it, I'm watching this again?
Always for us, hearing these stories, they're interesting and they're fun and we like some, we like that one.
We don't like others, right?
The question is always, how can we practice with this?

What is there in this to help me understand and see the ways that I'm enlightened and the ways that I'm caught and the ways that I'm confused and the ways that I'm not who I think I am and the ways that I really am who I think I am, right?
Because all of our thinking is also stories.
